guards.what: G1: Sign-aware power typing missing from Artifact interception (PowerCmd.apply's Artifact check uses the static power_cls.power_type class attribute instead of C#'s GetTypeForAmount(amount))
guards.issue: cmds.py:299 checks `power_cls.power_type == PowerType.DEBUFF` (a fixed class attribute) instead of C#'s sign-aware `canonicalPower.GetTypeForAmount(amount) != PowerType.Debuff` (ArtifactPower.cs:24; definition PowerModel.cs:460-471: `if (StackType==Counter && AllowNegative && amount<0) return Debuff;`). LIVE today: sts2_rl/monsters/glory/the_lost_and_forgotten.py:54,99 and sts2_rl/monsters/underdocks/lagavulin_matriarch.py:106-107 both apply negative StrengthPower/DexterityPower to the player as a Strength/Dexterity steal -- a Buff-typed (power_type=BUFF), allow_negative=True power applied with a negative amount, which C# classifies as Debuff and Artifact (if the player holds it) blocks and consumes a stack for. The sim's static check sees power_type==BUFF and skips the Artifact branch entirely, so the steal always lands even when the player has Artifact. Pinned with an xfail: test/test_hook_order.py::TestPowerCmdOrder::test_artifact_blocks_negative_signed_debuff.

guards.what: G2: Same sign-aware gap in UnsettlingLamp's own doubling condition, plus an amount<=0 early bail; currently dormant
guards.issue: sts2_rl/relics/unsettling_lamp.py:44-53's modify_power_amount bails on `amount <= 0` and then checks the static `power_cls.power_type != PowerType.DEBUFF`, instead of C#'s `power.GetTypeForAmount(amount) != PowerType.Debuff` (UnsettlingLamp.cs:124), which classifies a NEGATIVE amount on an AllowNegative buff (e.g. Strength/Dexterity) as Debuff and would double it. C#'s Malaise.cs:40 and Resonance.cs:33 both apply negative StrengthPower to an enemy with applier=player, cardSource=this -- exactly the shape Lamp is meant to double. Neither card is ported in the sim yet (grep confirms no sts2_rl/cards/*.py match for either name), so this is dormant, but it would misfire (fail to ever double) the instant either card is ported, since the sim's amount<=0 guard rejects ANY negative-amount application before the sign-aware check would even matter.

guards.what: G3: C#'s three ordered phases (BeforePowerAmountChanged event / ModifyPowerAmountGiven chain / ModifyPowerAmountReceived predicate chain) collapsed into one registration-order-dependent chain; Artifact bypasses the hook-listener system entirely
guards.issue: hooks.py:170-183's modify_power_amount is a single flat chain over hook-registration order with no phase separation, unlike C#'s three separately-sequenced calls (PowerCmd.cs:120,125,127) that guarantee given-before-received regardless of listener registration order. Additionally, ArtifactPower is not a modify_power_amount listener at all in the sim -- it is hard-coded as a direct block in cmds.py:299-306, outside the hook loop entirely (see its own docstring, sts2_rl/powers.py:315-325: 'This power has no active hook methods; it is intercepted by PowerCmd.apply'). The two general modify_power_amount listeners that DO exist -- UnsettlingLamp (given-side, debuff-only) and RuinedHelmet (received-side, StrengthPower-buff-only, sts2_rl/relics/ruined_helmet.py:23-39) -- are domain-disjoint today (one only touches debuffs, the other only touches a specific positive-amount buff), so no live collision is demonstrated. But nothing in the sim's architecture would enforce correct given-before-received ordering for two future listeners whose domains DO overlap, the way C#'s fixed three-call sequence does by construction.

Hook.cs declares AfterModifyingPowerAmountGiven (Hook.cs:796-809) and AfterModifyingPowerAmountReceived (Hook.cs:811-824), both of which the brief specifically flagged (2 of the 13 AfterModifying* variants Task 5's damage_pipeline audit found the sim implements only 1 of). The sim's hooks.py:170-183 modify_power_amount returns a bare aggregated int with no out-param modifiers list at all -- unlike its sibling modify_hp_lost/after_modify_hp_lost pair (hooks.py:126-154), which Task 5's re-audit found DOES carry this machinery (built for BufferPower). This is not merely a bookkeeping gap: ArtifactPower.AfterModifyingPowerAmountReceived (ArtifactPower.cs:38-41) is the actual method that calls PowerCmd.Decrement(this) in C# -- the sim reimplements that specific effect inline in cmds.py:301-305 (faithful in isolation, since Artifact is the only hard-coded listener), and RuinedHelmet's sim counterpart similarly folds its 'mark used' side effect directly into modify_power_amount (relics/ruined_helmet.py:37) instead of a separate after-hook. No SECOND listener currently needs the generic two-phase mechanism, so this is dormant beyond the two already-faithful special cases, but the general machinery the brief asked about is confirmed absent.

guards.what: G5: No PowerInstanceType (Instanced / InstancedPerApplier) distinction in FindExistingInstanceForStacking
guards.issue: PowerCmd.cs:165-174's FindExistingInstanceForStacking dispatches on power.InstanceType (PowerModel.cs:144, default None); the sim's stacking check (cmds.py:308, `if power_cls.id in target.powers`) always behaves as None (single shared instance per power id per owner) with no instance_type concept anywhere in the sim. Ten C# powers declare Instanced/InstancedPerApplier (grep of src/Core/Models/Powers/*.cs for 'InstanceType =>'); nine are ported: ToricToughnessPower and TheBombPower explicitly document the None-approximation and hand-roll a workaround bundling multiple logical instances inside one power's internal list (powers.py:1191-1200, 3748-3753). The other seven -- SwipePower, StranglePower (InstancedPerApplier, powers.py:2833-2869), AutomationPower, HeistPower, PanachePower, RollingBoulderPower, SandpitPower, ThieveryPower, WitheringPresencePower -- do not acknowledge the distinction in their docstrings or implementation at all. No currently-demonstrated collision (only one copy of each is realistically active on a given owner in present content), but a second simultaneous instance on the same owner (e.g. two Thieving Hoppers' Swipe on the same player, or Strangle applied to one target by two different appliers) would silently merge via on_stack in the sim where C# tracks them as independent instances.

guards.what: G6: No CombatManager.IsEnding / CanReceivePowers guard backstop anywhere in PowerCmd.apply
guards.issue: C#'s Apply<T> refuses to act once combat is ending (PowerCmd.cs:69-72, spec step 1) or against a creature CanReceivePowers says no to (PowerCmd.cs:73-76, spec step 2 -- CanReceivePowers reuses Hook.ShouldAllowHitting, Creature.cs:308-322, the SAME predicate damage_pipeline's guard N1 covers for the damage path), both as hard backstops independent of caller discipline; ModifyAmount separately re-checks IsEnding (PowerCmd.cs:217-220, step 24). The sim's PowerCmd.apply (cmds.py:270-332) has none of these guards at any point in its single code path. should_allow_hitting IS wired into the sim's damage pipeline (DamageCmd.deal, per damage_pipeline's N1) but not into PowerCmd.apply -- so a currently-unhittable creature (e.g. a mid-revival Decimillipede segment) could still receive a power application in the sim where C# would refuse it outright. No concrete broken interaction is demonstrated (spot-checked callers apply powers only to already-resolved targets), matching the same defense-in-depth-absence pattern as damage_pipeline's guard G5.

guards.what: N1: IsVisible is entirely absent from the sim's Power model; C#'s power.IsVisible gate (UnsettlingLamp.cs:93, ArtifactPower.cs:29-33) provably never varies
guards.rationale: A full grep of src/Core/Models/Powers/*.cs for `IsVisibleInternal` (the only way to override the default-true PowerModel.IsVisible, PowerModel.cs:150-167) returns zero matches anywhere in the entire C# codebase -- not just Ironclad-scope. IsVisible is therefore provably always true for every power in the current game, in both the Lamp's own latch gate and Artifact's own intercept gate. The sim's total omission of the concept produces no currently observable divergence, and cannot until new C# content introduces an invisible power (which would itself require a source-code change upstream, not just an unported-content gap) -- this is dead code in the source itself, not merely unported.

guards.what: N2: TemporaryStrengthPower/TemporaryDexterityPower's internal wrapped-power application omits applier in the sim instead of C#'s explicit HasDoubledTemporaryPowerSource double-dip guard
guards.rationale: C#'s TemporaryStrengthPower.BeforeApplied (TemporaryStrengthPower.cs:146-156) re-applies its InternallyAppliedPower (StrengthPower) via a full separate PowerCmd.Apply<T> call carrying the SAME applier/cardSource as the wrapper's own application, which would let UnsettlingLamp double both the wrapper (e.g. ManglePower, a Debuff) AND the internal StrengthPower independently (quadrupling) without UnsettlingLamp.HasDoubledTemporaryPowerSource (UnsettlingLamp.cs:164-167) explicitly detecting and skipping the second doubling. The sim's TemporaryStrengthPower/TemporaryDexterityPower counterparts (powers.py:840-870, 920-940) instead OMIT the applier parameter entirely on the internal StrengthPower/DexterityPower application (`PowerCmd.apply(hooks, owner, StrengthPower, self._sign * amount)`, no applier= kwarg) -- since UnsettlingLamp's own modify_power_amount requires `applier is self.player` to trigger at all, the applier-less internal call is naturally skipped, achieving the same 'double once, not twice' outcome by a different mechanism. Traced through both the wrapper-doubled and internal-application steps by hand for the ported Mangle case: both codebases net -6 Strength from a 3-stack Mangle with Lamp active. Verified equivalent for currently-ported content; recorded as a deliberate-divergence rather than faithful because the mechanisms genuinely differ and a future power with a DIFFERENT double-dip shape could expose it.

guards.what: N3: Artifact's owner-scoping (target != base.Owner in C#, a hook-iteration self-filter) vs the sim's direct target.powers.get("artifact") lookup
guards.rationale: C#'s ArtifactPower.TryModifyPowerAmountReceived is discovered via IterateCombatHookListeners (iterating every hook-listening model in the whole combat) and self-filters with `if (target != base.Owner) return false` (ArtifactPower.cs:19-23) to only intercept when the power is being applied to Artifact's own owner. The sim's cmds.py:300 `target.powers.get("artifact")` directly looks up whether the TARGET (not some other creature) holds Artifact -- architecturally a special case instead of a hook-iteration self-filter, but semantically identical: both only ever have the target's own Artifact stack intercept a debuff aimed at that same target.

guards.what: N4: ModifyAmount's missing CanReceivePowers check (spec step 25) is a faithful absence, not a divergence
guards.rationale: C#'s ModifyAmount (PowerCmd.cs:215-271) itself only checks combatState==null, never CanReceivePowers, unlike Apply<T>/Apply(power,...) which check it twice (steps 2, 16). The sim's stacking branch (cmds.py:308-321) likewise has no CanReceivePowers-equivalent check -- both codebases omit it identically in the re-stacking path, so this is not a sim-vs-C# divergence at all, merely an asymmetry already present within the C# source between its own two power-application pipelines.
